analysis.one_liner: Lets student loans be wiped out in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Judiciary Committee after 19 members from both parties signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, people carrying student debt can only cancel those loans in bankruptcy if they prove repaying them would cause an 'undue hardship' — a very high bar. This bill would delete that rule, so student loans could be discharged in bankruptcy the same way credit card debt or medical debt can. It was introduced by a Maryland Democrat with bipartisan cosponsors, but the House Judiciary Committee never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers whose finances have collapsed and who would otherwise carry student debt for life. About 1.3 trillion dollars in student debt was outstanding at the time, and borrowers stuck in default or permanent hardship would get the same fresh-start option available to people with other kinds of debt.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the bankruptcy code's special carve-out for educational loans, making them dischargeable like other unsecured debt [S3].
Removes the 'undue hardship' test that currently makes student debt nearly impossible to cancel in bankruptcy [S2].
Applies to bankruptcy cases filed after enactment, giving a clean start going forward [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders — including private lenders and the federal loan program — would absorb losses when borrowers discharge debt in bankruptcy. Those losses could come back as higher interest rates or tighter credit for future students, and discharges on federal loans would fall partly on taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan lenders and federal loan program

drawbacks.text: Easier discharge shifts losses to lenders and, for federal loans, to taxpayers, which could push lenders to charge higher rates or lend less to risky students [S2].

The hardship standard, though harsh, exists to protect the loan system and taxpayers from borrowers who could repay walking away from debt; removing it entirely eliminates any screening rather than loosening it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is real for the small share of borrowers in genuine financial collapse, for whom bankruptcy is the only escape from unpayable debt. The costs are spread widely — slightly higher borrowing costs for future students and losses for lenders and taxpayers — and the bill offers no middle-ground screening, simply treating student debt like any other debt. A reasonable trade on its merits, but it never got the chance to be debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Judiciary Committee and its subcommittee for two years and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Delaney introduced the bill on January 21, 2015 [S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S5].
On February 5, 2015, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
It gathered 17 cosponsors, 15 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders and the federal student loan program, which kept their bankruptcy protection; borrowers in hardship got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Student loan lenders kept their protection

for.name: Rep. John Delaney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.

for.name: 17 cosponsors (15 House Democrats, 2 House Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support.

against.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it stayed in committee for the full two-year Congress.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action beyond a routine subcommittee referral two weeks after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsors were bipartisan — 15 Democrats and 2 Republicans — but the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee, which controls whether bills get hearings, never acted on it.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders (private lenders and the federal loan program)
industries.note: These lenders rely on the undue-hardship rule to keep student debt nearly escape-proof; the bill would have let borrowers discharge the debt in bankruptcy, transferring losses back to lenders and the federal loan book. Their interest in keeping the rule runs directly against borrowers in financial distress.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Dischargeable debt ends servicing revenue and collection activity on wiped-out balances, so these companies had an interest in the bill never advancing. They are downstream of the same carve-out the bill repeals.
